dataset_family: Duke University iMIND study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03233646 = Duke IRB Pro00082598, linked on p.2 of P-363). 80 MCI (NIA-AA, memory neurologist) + 129 cognitively normal (community / Duke ADRC registry). P-363 and P-1317 come from the same family, and the family counts once. Registry stubs: P-246 (duplicate_of P-163, though its block describes a fluid-biomarker systematic review) and P-247 (whose block describes this Wisely CNN paper although its duplicate_of says P-146). The pointers look misattached, and neither stub adds anything.
method_family: Deep learning (multimodal CNN, ResNet18 transfer learning) on OCT GC-IPL thickness maps plus OCTA superficial capillary plexus images plus image-derived quantitative OCT/OCTA metrics; eye-level MCI-vs-CN classification on a subject-disjoint internal test set with stochastic age matching
what_it_shows: Wisely et al. 2023, Ophthalmology Science. A multimodal CNN on OCT GC-IPL maps, OCTA images and image-derived quantitative data separated MCI from CN eyes on a subject-disjoint internal test set: AUC 0.809 (95% CI 0.681-0.937), sensitivity 79%, specificity 83%. The mean AUC over 10 random re-splits was 0.828. Image-only models were weaker (GC-IPL 0.681, OCTA 0.625, both 0.693). It is single-centre with no external validation, and the unit is the eye.
why: PDF identity confirmed: the title, the authors (Wisely, Richardson, Henao, Robbins, Ma, Wang, Johnson, Liu, Grewal, Fekrat) and DOI 10.1016/j.xops.2023.100355 match the block, whose header is only the filename but whose content describes this CNN. I read the whole extract through the references. STATED FORM, partly: its own within-study classifier supports retinal structure (OCT/OCTA) as a biomarker direction for MCI detection. It does not test scalability; it uses specialist Zeiss Cirrus OCT/OCTA with manual quality exclusion, and 'widely available' is asserted in the introduction only. NARROWED FORM, yes: the headline is 'preliminary, single-centre associations with MCI; retinal imaging discriminated MCI'. The study itself discriminates clinically diagnosed MCI from CN on retinal imaging at a single centre with no external validation (the authors say this is still to come, p.7). Admitting it widens the named scope from 'fundus with or without OCT ... in two small Chinese hospital cohorts' to OCT/OCTA in a US cohort. Design strengths relative to P-5 and P-952: subject-disjoint splits (p.4) and an age-matched test set. CAVEATS FROM THE PDF: (1) Small test set: 30 MCI eyes and 60 control eyes, with about 80% of the MCI eyes age-matched per run. The evaluation is per eye, so fellow eyes within the test set are correlated and the CI is probably too narrow. (2) Anomaly: the image-derived quantitative-data model alone scored AUC 0.960, above the full model. Yet in the GEE comparisons (age and sex adjusted) mean GC-IPL (P = 0.778) and RNFL (P = 0.731) do not differ, and most OCTA metrics do not either (only 3-mm-ring PD, P < 0.001, with an unusual SD of 0.10 vs 0.03). The source of that signal is unexplained. (3) The full cohort is age-imbalanced (72.5 vs 68.6 y, P < 0.001), handled only by post hoc test-set matching (the authors call this a limitation, p.7). (4) Sex (44.8% vs 30.1% male) and education (15.6 vs 17.2 y) also differ; demographics were excluded from the best model but can shape the images. INDEPENDENCE: no overlap with P-5 (Daping/WMU), P-952 (Shenzhen), P-966 (GARD Korea) or P-105. It is the same Duke study as P-1317 (IRB Pro00082598) and P-363 (NCT03233646 plus Pro00082598), and all three share Robbins, Grewal and Fekrat. Choose one Duke paper to represent the family, and count it once. Not a preprint: peer-reviewed Ophthalmology Science article. The Elsevier extract renders CI dashes as 'e' (e.g. '0.681e0.937'); I read them as ranges.

quotes.quote: Images from 236 eyes of 129 cognitively normal subjects and 154 eyes of 80 MCI subjects were used for training, validating, and testing the CNN. When applied to the independent test set using inputs including GC-IPL thickness maps, OCTA images, and quantitative OCT and OCTA data, the AUC value for the CNN was 0.809 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.681–0.937). This model achieved a sensitivity of 79% and specificity of 83%.

Models using quantitative data alone were also tested, with a model using quantitative data derived from images, 0.960 (95% CI: 0.902–1.00), outperforming a model using demographic data alone, 0.580 (95% CI: 0.417–0.742).
The images obtained for CNN input were from an ongoing clinical trial (Clinicaltrials.gov, NCT03233646) approved by Duke University Health System's institutional review board.

Subjects with MCI were diagnosed based on clinical history, cognitive testing, and any available neuroimaging by an expert neurologist (A.L.) with specialization in memory disorders. All diagnoses were made in accordance with National Institute on Aging and Alzheimer's Association guidelines.

In order to account for age as a potential confounding variable between the MCI and control groups, stochastic age-matching for the test dataset was employed before each model run; 80% of the MCI eyes in the test dataset were randomly selected, and, for each MCI eye, the control eye with the nearest age was also added to the age-matched test dataset.

One hundred four (68%) MCI eyes were used for training, 20 (13%) were used for validation, and 30 (19%) were used for testing. There was no patient overlap between the training, validation, and test groups, and patients were randomly assigned to each group.
we reassigned eyes randomly to the training, validation, and testing groups in 10 variations and ran the CNN for each grouping, resulting in a mean AUC of 0.828 and standard deviation of 0.035.
